title: Optimizely Platform Hit by Large-Scale Malicious Script Injection; 178 Brand Websites Affected, Crypto Wallets Lose $7,000
text:
Optimizely Platform Hit by Large-Scale Malicious Script Injection; 178 Brand Websites Affected, Crypto Wallets Lose $7,000 — BigGo Finance Ask AI Real-time News Market Earnings Call Event Calendar Watchlist Podcast Market Influencers Earnings Call Event Calendar Watchlist Podcast Market Influencers More Ask AI Real-time News Watchlist Holdings Market Earnings Call Event Calendar Podcast Market Influencers Optimizely Platform Hit by Large-Scale Malicious Script Injection; 178 Brand Websites Affected, Crypto Wallets Lose $7,000
 Add preferred source Security researcher Scott Helme reported that on November 16, attackers used the A/B testing platform Optimizely Web to write malicious JavaScript into the "Project JavaScript" field of customers' backends. Delivered through the company's official CDN, the scripts affected roughly 178 organizations and 188 scripts, including the official websites of Zoom, BBC, CNN, HSBC, Salesforce, GitLab, IKEA, Equifax, Peacock, and Fox News. The malicious scripts could replace cryptocurrency payment addresses, skim credit card numbers, steal cookies and screenshots, and attempt to plant exploit code on iOS devices. As of 19:25 UTC that day, the attacker's wallet had received about $7,000. Optimizely spokesperson Victoria Johnson said the company had blocked the vulnerable path, deployed a fix, and notified affected customers. Key Elements 
 Optimizely Scott Helme Report URI Zoom BBC CNN HSBC Salesforce GitLab IKEA Peacock Fox News Equifax Victoria Johnson Security researchers have disclosed a malicious script injection incident launched through the A/B testing platform Optimizely Web, affecting about 178 organizations and a total of 188 infected scripts. The official websites of well-known brands including Zoom, BBC, CNN, HSBC, Salesforce, GitLab, IKEA, Equifax, Peacock, and Fox News all served malicious JavaScript to visitors.
 According to a November 16 report by security researcher Scott Helme, attackers wrote malicious code into the "Project JavaScript" field of customers' Optimizely backends. These scripts were then delivered normally through Optimizely's official CDN, effectively bypassing most websites' content trust mechanisms. The brands' own core code was never touched, yet visitors were exposed to risk.
 The malicious scripts had a wide range of functions, including replacing cryptocurrency payment addresses on pages with the attacker's own wallet, skimming card numbers as users entered credit card details, stealing cookies and screenshots, and attempting to plant exploit code on iOS devices. As of 19:25 UTC on November 16, the attacker's wallet had received the equivalent of about $7,000 in cryptocurrency, with nearly all of it arriving within roughly nine hours that day.
 Optimizely spokesperson Victoria Johnson, responding to media inquiries, said the company "identified a security incident in which unauthorized parties exploited a vulnerability in the Experimentation account registration flow" and had notified all affected customers. The party also added malicious JavaScript to some customer projects, but the company "has blocked the vulnerable path and deployed a fix."
 Notably, Report URI, which first disclosed the incident, itself sells malicious script detection services, and the scale and details of the event still await further independent verification. Another threat intelligence firm, Mallory, also tracked the case and alleged that endpoints of other ad-tech platforms had likewise delivered problematic scripts.
 Below is a summary of the known scope and losses of this incident:
 Item Details 
 Affected organizations About 178 (188 infected scripts) 
 Major affected brands Zoom, BBC, CNN, HSBC, Salesforce, GitLab, IKEA, Equifax, Peacock, Fox News, NPR, Air France-KLM 
 Malicious behavior Replacing cryptocurrency addresses, skimming credit card numbers, stealing cookies and screenshots, iOS exploitation 
 Attacker wallet receipts About $7,000 as of 19:25 UTC on November 16 
 Platform response Blocked vulnerable path, deployed fix, notified affected customers 
 Note: The number of affected organizations and the dollar amounts are figures reported by security researchers; final losses are still being assessed.
 The incident has also prompted a fresh look at the trust boundaries of third-party marketing and experimentation platforms. Such tools are typically onboarded by marketing or growth teams themselves, and to launch tests quickly they often skip the engineering team's code review process. Once a vulnerability appears on the platform side, it effectively opens a direct path for attackers to the official websites of major brands. For large websites, third-party scripts have long been regarded as one of the hardest parts of the supply chain to control. The scale of this incident is rare, but based on the financial losses disclosed so far, the impact leans more toward cleanup burdens for system administrators than a massive theft.
 For corporate security teams, the next priorities will be checking whether their websites still load unreviewed third-party scripts, auditing Optimizely project permissions, and confirming whether payment pages ever displayed abnormal cryptocurrency address replacements. For investors, the incident itself is not yet enough to shake the financial performance of the companies involved, but the security and liability allocation of third-party SaaS tools are expected to become more heavily weighted conditions in corporate procurement and contract negotiations.
